problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
Summary

a. Verdict: I have successfully solved the problem. The final answer is \boxed{4048}.

b. Method Sketch: We view the grid as the bipartite graph K_{n,n} with rows and columns as the two vertex classes. The uncovered squares form a perfect matching M. A rectangular tile corresponds to a complete bipartite subgraph (biclique) whose edge set avoids M. Using a critical‑edge argument we show that any partition of the edges of K_{n,n} without the matching edges into bicliques needs at least 2n-2 bicliques. Then we exhibit a partition with exactly 2n-2 bicliques: n-1 stars centred at the columns and n-1 stars centred at the rows, which translate into vertical and horizontal strips of unit width/height. This yields the optimal number of tiles.

Detailed Solution

1. Reformulation. Let n = 2025. Because each row and each column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the set of uncovered squares is a permutation matrix: there exists a bijection p : {1,…,n} → {1,…,n} such that the uncovered square in row i lies in column p(i). All other n^2 - n unit squares must be covered by axis‑parallel rectangular tiles that do not contain any uncovered square. For a fixed permutation p we denote by f(p) the smallest number of tiles needed to cover the complement of the permutation matrix. The quantity asked for in the problem is F(n) = min_{p} f(p). We shall prove that F(n) = 2n - 2 for every n ≥ 2, and therefore F(2025) = 2·2025 - 2 = 4048.

2. Lower bound of 2n - 2 tiles.

Define left‑critical cells. For each column c with 1 \le c \le n-1 let i_c be the unique row such that p(i_c) = c+1 (such a row exists because p is a permutation). The cell (i_c , c) lies strictly to the left of the uncovered square (i_c , c+1) in its row; we call it a left‑critical cell. Any rectangle that covers a left‑critical cell cannot extend to column c+1, otherwise it would also contain the uncovered square (i_c , c+1). Consequently the rightmost column of such a rectangle is exactly c.

Suppose a single rectangle covered two distinct left‑critical cells (i_c , c) and (i_{c'} , c') with c < c'. Because the rectangle contains column c' its column set contains every column between its leftmost column and c', in particular column c+1. The row i_c belongs to the rectangle, so the rectangle would contain the uncovered square (i_c , c+1), a contradiction. Hence no rectangle can contain two different left‑critical cells. Since there are n-1 left‑critical cells, at least n-1 rectangles are required to cover them.

Define right‑critical cells analogously. For each column c with 2 \le c \le n let j_c be the unique row such that p(j_c) = c-1. The cell (j_c , c) lies strictly to the right of the uncovered square (j_c , c-1) in its row; we call it a right‑critical cell. By the same argument, a rectangle covering a right‑critical cell cannot extend to column c-1, so its leftmost column is exactly c, and no rectangle can contain two different right‑critical cells. There are again n-1 right‑critical cells, so at least n-1 additional rectangles are needed.

Thus any tiling of the complement of a permutation matrix uses at least (n-1)+(n-1) = 2n-2 rectangles. Hence

F(n) \ge 2n-2.   (1)

3. Construction attaining 2n-2 rectangles.

Take the identity permutation p(i)=i for all i. The uncovered squares are precisely the diagonal cells (i,i), i=1,…,n.

For each column c with 1 \le c \le n-1 define the vertical strip

R_c = { (i,c) : i = c+1, c+2, … , n }.

Geometrically R_c is a rectangle of width 1 and height n-c whose upper side lies on the grid line just below the diagonal cell (c,c). Because the strip contains only rows strictly larger than c, it does not contain the diagonal cell (c,c) and therefore does not contain any uncovered square.

For each row r with 1 \le r \le n-1 define the horizontal strip

C_r = { (r,j) : j = r+1, r+2, … , n }.

Geometrically C_r is a rectangle of height 1 and width n-r whose left side lies on the grid line just to the right of the diagonal cell (r,r). Since the strip contains only columns strictly larger than r, it avoids the uncovered square (r,r).

The family {R_c : 1 \le c \le n-1} \cup {C_r : 1 \le r \le n-1} consists of exactly 2n-2 rectangles. They are pairwise disjoint: a cell with i > j belongs to the unique vertical strip R_j and to no horizontal strip, while a cell with i < j belongs to the unique horizontal strip C_i and to no vertical strip. The diagonal cells (i,i) are uncovered by construction. Consequently the 2n-2 rectangles cover every unit square except the required one per row and column.

Thus we have exhibited a tiling with 2n-2 tiles, showing that

F(n) \le 2n-2.   (2)

4. Conclusion.

From (1) and (2) we obtain F(n) = 2n-2 for all n \ge 2. For n = 2025 this yields

2\cdot2025 - 2 = 4048.

Hence the minimum possible number of tiles is \boxed{4048}.
